family_history: No known family history of dementia or FTD
Father: died of myocardial infarction at age 78
Mother: alive at age 87, cognitively intact

social_history.occupation: Retired accountant (retired 2 years ago after 35 years); formerly managed accounts for a multinational firm
social_history.alcohol: Rare social drinking, less than 1 drink per week
social_history.marital_status: Widowed, lives with adult son and daughter-in-law

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Cooperative. Speaks fluent, grammatically intact English and Mandarin (per family). MoCA 20/30: loses 4 points on delayed recall (1/5), 2 on executive tasks (serial 7s intact but trails A–B poor, 1-letter fluency 6 words in 60s), 2 on orientation (day and date), 1 on naming. Notably, she cannot identify photographs of her son's work colleagues whom she met repeatedly over 5 years (prosopagnosia evident on informal bedside testing with family photos). When shown a photo of a former colleague named Mr. Chen, she describes him as 'a middle-aged man' but cannot recall his identity. She recognises familiar objects normally. She correctly identifies all basic geometric shapes and reads printed words without difficulty.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Visual acuity 20/25 bilaterally with current spectacles. Visual fields: full to confrontation bilaterally. Extraocular movements: full, no nystagmus. Pupils: equal, round, reactive bilaterally. Facial sensation intact. Facial strength symmetric. Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. No dysarthria.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone. Strength 5/5 throughout all extremities, bilateral and symmetric. No tremor. No rigidity. No fasciculations. No alien-limb phenomenon. No apraxia of either hand.
neurological_exam.sensory: Normal to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception bilaterally. No cortical sensory loss. No extinction to double simultaneous stimulation.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric throughout all extremities. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Bilateral palmomental reflexes present. Snout reflex present. Grasp reflex absent.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact finger-nose, heel-shin. Normal rapid alternating movements bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence, stride, and arm swing. No parkinsonian features. Tandem gait intact.
neurological_exam.additional: Son and daughter-in-law report a 2-year history of gradual but striking change in personality and behavior. The patient was formerly a meticulous, warm, socially engaged woman who maintained close friendships and was known for her attentiveness to family members. Over the past 2 years, the family first noticed she could no longer recognise the faces of neighbors she had known for decades, mistook a long-standing friend for a stranger, and on one occasion failed to recognise her own son when he arrived with a beard. Family initially brought her to an ophthalmologist 6 months ago, believing she had a vision problem. The ophthalmologist found no primary visual pathology and noted that she read normally and navigated the office independently. Concurrently, the family has observed significant personality change: she has become emotionally flat and unresponsive to distress in family members, failing to comfort her daughter-in-law during a bereavement. The son reports she now appears completely indifferent to the death of a close friend. She has developed rigid daily routines — insisting on eating congee at exactly the same time every morning and watching the same three television programs in sequence each day. She becomes visibly agitated if the routine is disrupted. She has lost interest in activities she formerly enjoyed (gardening, mahjong with friends). The son initially attributed these changes to grief (her husband died 3 years ago) and sought a psychiatric evaluation 4 months ago. The psychiatrist diagnosed major depressive disorder and started sertraline 50 mg daily. After 3 months there has been no improvement in the family's estimation; the routine behaviors and face-recognition failure have worsened. She herself does not complain of sadness, does not describe hopelessness, and has not lost appetite. She denies recognising any difficulty, expressing no concern about her inability to identify faces.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive inability to recognise familiar faces and personality change — 2 years (reported by family); referred after failed ophthalmology evaluation and inadequate antidepressant response
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. L is a 64-year-old right-handed retired East Asian accountant brought to the neurology clinic by her son and daughter-in-law after a 2-year course of gradually progressive behavioral change and loss of face and person recognition. The family's initial concern was her repeated failure to recognise the faces of neighbors, family friends, and even briefly-disguised family members (e.g., son arriving with a beard), which they interpreted as a vision problem. She was referred to ophthalmology 6 months ago, where visual acuity, fields, and eye movement examination were normal and no primary ocular pathology was found. Despite reassurance, face-recognition failure has continued and the family has now noted additional features: she can no longer recall the personal histories of people she knew well — she does not remember that her neighbor Mrs. Park lost her husband last year, that a close friend relocated, or any biographic facts about colleagues she worked alongside for decades. She describes these individuals as 'unfamiliar' even when told their names. In contrast, she continues to recognise famous landmark faces shown to her from Chinese television news without difficulty (overlearned public figures). Object naming, basic word-finding in conversation, and reading remain intact. Concurrent personality change has been progressive: she has lost empathy for family distress, shows no grief response to interpersonal losses, and has developed stereotyped daily routines with marked agitation when these are disrupted. She fixates on specific television programs and food preferences. These behavioral features prompted a psychiatric evaluation 4 months ago, resulting in a diagnosis of major depression (attributed to widowhood) and initiation of sertraline 50 mg. After 3 months, behavioral symptoms and face-recognition failure have not improved. She herself does not endorse depressed mood, hopelessness, guilt, or anhedonia beyond routine preferences; she lacks insight into her cognitive or social difficulties. Past medical history includes well-controlled hypertension, osteopenia, and mild hyperlipidemia. No family history of dementia. Never smoked. No significant alcohol use. Medications: losartan 50 mg, rosuvastatin 10 mg, calcium/vitamin D, sertraline 50 mg (initiated 3 months ago). Allergy: penicillin (rash).

findings.location: Right anterior temporal lobe, including temporal pole, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex; markedly asymmetric right greater than left

signal_characteristics.T1: Severe volume loss of the right temporal pole and adjacent anterior temporal neocortex with marked gyral thinning and sulcal widening; right amygdala appears reduced in volume. Left anterior temporal lobe shows only mild volume loss in comparison.
signal_characteristics.T2_FLAIR: No intraparenchymal signal abnormality within the atrophic regions; no hyperintense signal in the temporal poles

signal_characteristics.T1: Right hippocampus mildly reduced in volume, with preservation of internal architecture. Left hippocampus normal volume for age. Entorhinal cortex atrophy more marked on the right.
Mild bilateral frontal sulcal widening within age-expected range; no disproportionate frontal atrophy. Right orbitofrontal cortex shows borderline volume loss.

findings.location: Parietal, occipital lobes, posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus

signal_characteristics.T1: Normal cortical thickness and sulcal pattern bilaterally; no atrophy. No inferior parietal or angular gyrus atrophy.

signal_characteristics.T2_FLAIR: Fazekas grade 1 periventricular punctate hyperintensities bilaterally — non-confluent, non-specific, within expected range for age and vascular risk factors

signal_characteristics.DWI: No restricted diffusion. No cortical ribboning.

volumetrics.hippocampal_volume: Right mildly reduced; left within normal limits

additional_observations: Markedly asymmetric right-predominant anterior temporal atrophy
Relative sparing of posterior cortex, parietal and occipital lobes
No mass lesion, hemorrhage, or acute ischemia
No hydrocephalus; ventricular size proportionate to cortical atrophy
mri.impression: Severe right-predominant anterior temporal atrophy including temporal pole, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex, with mild left anterior temporal involvement. Posterior cortex preserved. Fazekas grade 1 non-confluent periventricular white matter changes

labs.interpretation: All values within normal limits. No metabolic, thyroid, nutritional, infectious, or reversible cause of cognitive decline identified.

findings.finding: Severe hypometabolism of the right temporal pole and anterior temporal neocortex (including right superior and middle temporal gyri anteriorly, right amygdala region, and right parahippocampal gyrus anteriorly). Estimated 31% reduction in FDG uptake versus cerebellar reference. This is the most prominent metabolic deficit.
Mild-to-moderate right orbitofrontal hypometabolism (14% reduction), extending into right anterior insula.
Mild hypometabolism of the left temporal pole (9% reduction) — substantially less than the contralateral side.
Preserved — posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, parietal association cortex, and occipital lobes show normal FDG uptake bilaterally.
Mild hypometabolism consistent with structural changes; left hippocampal metabolism normal.

output.impression: Severe right-predominant anterior temporal hypometabolism with additional mild right orbitofrontal involvement — a markedly asymmetric temporal pattern with relative preservation of posterior cortex. Posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus metabolism are preserved

findings.finding: Face recognition (Benton Facial Recognition Test): 30/54 (<2nd percentile, severely impaired). Unable to match photographs of the same unfamiliar faces from different angles. Contrasts with preserved object recognition (pictures of common objects: 100% correct).

Person-specific semantic knowledge (Famous Faces naming and biographical recall, East Asian celebrity cohort): Correctly identified 9/30 famous faces (30th percentile — low, with partial credit for naming without biographical knowledge). For personally known individuals (family photos test): identified 5/8 by face alone, but relied heavily on contextual cues (uniform, setting).

Empathy and social cognition (Interpersonal Reactivity Index — informant form, NPI-Q — informant): IRI empathic concern subscale rated by son: 4/28 (severely reduced). NPI-Q: apathy/indifference 6/12, disinhibition 4/12, aberrant motor behavior (rituals/repetitive) 6/12.

Behavioral inventory (Frontal Behavioral Inventory, FBI — informant): Total score 26/72. Elevated on apathy (7/12), perseveration (8/12), and personal neglect (6/12) subscales. Verbal disinhibition subscale low (2/12).
Executive function (DKEFS Trails switching, Color-Word Interference): Moderately impaired. Trails switching: 8th percentile. Color-word inhibition: 12th percentile.
Object naming (Boston Naming Test): 49/60 (25th percentile — low average). No word-finding failure for common objects. Single-word comprehension: intact.

Episodic memory (HVLT-R): Immediate recall 9/12 trials 1–3 (35th percentile). Delayed recall 7/12 (30th percentile). Recognition 11/12 (55th percentile). Episodic memory is modestly impaired but recognition is relatively preserved.
Visuospatial (Rey-O copy, Block design): Copy 32/36 (60th percentile — normal). Block design WAIS-IV scaled score 9 (37th percentile — average). No visuospatial deficit.
Language: Fluent speech, intact grammar, no paraphasias. Single-word comprehension intact. Category fluency (animals): 11 in 60 s (20th percentile). No surface dyslexia on reading test.

output.impression: Neuropsychological profile distinguished by severe impairment in face recognition and person-specific semantic knowledge, markedly reduced empathy per informant, and moderately impaired executive function — with relative preservation of object naming, visuospatial function, and language. Episodic memory mildly impaired with preserved recognition. Pattern indicates a right anterior-temporal-predominant deficit: associative (agnosic) face recognition impairment with intact visuospatial processing — not a primary visual deficit

results.title: Sensitivity of revised diagnostic criteria for the behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia
results.finding: Rascovsky et al. 2011: bvFTD diagnostic criteria require ≥3 of 6 core features — early behavioral disinhibition, apathy/inertia, loss of empathy/sympathy, perseverative/stereotyped behavior, hyperorality/dietary changes, executive dysfunction. Frontotemporal atrophy or hypometabolism on neuroimaging supports 'probable' bvFTD.

results.title: FDG-PET improves accuracy in distinguishing frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease
results.finding: Foster et al. 2007: FDG-PET accurately distinguishes frontotemporal hypometabolism (frontal and anterior temporal predominant) from the temporoparietal and posterior cingulate pattern of Alzheimer's disease. Posterior cingulate cortex preservation is a key feature distinguishing FTD from AD.

results.title: Frontotemporal dementia
results.finding: Bang et al. 2015: Right temporal-predominant FTD presents with prosopagnosia (impaired face recognition), loss of person-specific semantic knowledge, prominent empathy loss, and complex repetitive behaviors. Language (grammar, fluency) is characteristically spared early. The anatomic substrate is right anterior temporal neocortex and amygdala, distinct from left-predominant semantic dementia/svPPA which presents primarily with word comprehension and object knowledge loss.

output.summary: Right temporal-predominant bvFTD is characterized by prosopagnosia (associative face agnosia) and loss of person-specific semantic memory, stemming from right anterior temporal lobe and amygdala degeneration. Rascovsky 2011 criteria require ≥3 core behavioral features within 3 years and neuroimaging support for 'probable' bvFTD. FDG-PET (Foster 2007) demonstrating anterior temporal hypometabolism with preserved posterior cingulate distinguishes this from Alzheimer-type patterns. Empathy loss, repetitive behaviors, and apathy — alongside face/person-knowledge deficits — constitute the characteristic syndrome. There is no primary visual processing deficit; the face-recognition failure is associative (right anterior temporal) rather than perceptual (occipito-parietal).

findings.finding: NEGATIVE for amyloid plaque burden. No significant cortical amyloid deposition in frontal, temporal, parietal, or occipital regions. SUVr values in all neocortical regions are below the established positivity threshold.

differential.diagnosis: Alzheimer disease (atypical, posterior cortical or early amnestic variant)
differential.key_features: AD can produce right temporal atrophy and agnosia; differentiated by FDG pattern (posterior cingulate sparing) and negative amyloid biomarkers.

svPPA involves anterior temporal atrophy but is typically left-predominant with single-word comprehension loss; this patient has right-predominant atrophy with prosopagnosia and intact word comprehension.

Family's initial attribution and prior antidepressant trial; distinguished by lack of subjective depressed mood, absence of neurovegetative symptoms, progressive behavioral/imaging findings, and failure of antidepressant.
Only Fazekas 1 non-confluent white matter changes; no strategic infarct in right temporal region; lobar degenerative pattern not explained by vascular burden.
Ophthalmology evaluation normal; visual acuity 20/25, full visual fields; object recognition and visuospatial function intact — face-recognition failure is associative, not perceptual.

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise anterior temporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; no parkinsonism is present. Not indicated in this case.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once structural MRI and FDG-PET have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural cause of focal cognitive symptoms and screen for elevated ICP before lumbar puncture.

critical_actions: Recognise that prosopagnosia in this context is associative face agnosia from right anterior temporal degeneration — not a primary visual deficit; do not pursue primary ophthalmologic workup for the face-recognition failure.

Distinguish FTD apathy from major depression: FTD apathy lacks subjective dysphoria, hopelessness, guilt, and neurovegetative symptoms; failure of a prior antidepressant trial with ongoing behavioral progression argues strongly against primary depression.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) — this patient meets: loss of empathy, perseverative/stereotyped behaviors, and apathy/inertia.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given behavioral changes and insight impairment.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Discuss discontinuation of sertraline given lack of response and FTD diagnosis confirmed.
contraindicated_actions: Do not refer for primary ophthalmologic workup (retina, visual cortex, refraction) as the sole evaluation for the face-recognition complaint — the ophthalmology evaluation is already documented as normal, and the deficit is an associative agnosia, not a perceptual disorder.
Do not continue or escalate antidepressant therapy as the primary treatment for behavioral symptoms without completing the dementia workup — treating FTD apathy as depression delays diagnosis.
Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
key_reasoning_points: Prosopagnosia in right temporal FTD is associative (agnosic): the patient cannot assign identity to a correctly-perceived face, distinguishable from perceptual face processing failure by intact object recognition, normal visuospatial testing, and a normal ophthalmology evaluation — the deficit localises to right anterior temporal neocortex, not visual cortex.

Right-predominant anterior temporal atrophy and hypometabolism are the neuroimaging correlates: all imaging findings must be right-sided; the presence of right-sided findings (not left) is what drives prosopagnosia and person-knowledge loss.

Apathy-vs-depression distinction is clinically critical: FTD apathy presents without subjective sadness, hopelessness, or guilt; neurovegetative features are absent or non-specific; antidepressants fail to improve the behavioral syndrome; progressive imaging changes are incompatible with primary mood disorder.

Person-specific semantic knowledge loss (losing biographical facts about known individuals) is a distinct right temporal-predominant feature, anatomically dissociated from left-sided word comprehension loss seen in svPPA.
Preserved posterior cingulate cortex metabolism on FDG-PET (the AD signature region) is a critical distinguishing feature from Alzheimer's disease in a patient with temporal atrophy.
Negative amyloid biomarkers remove the primary differential concern of atypical AD; right temporal FTD-spectrum is the supported diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Family initially brought patient to ophthalmology for 'vision problem' and ophthalmology found no primary ocular pathology
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could anchor the diagnostic workup on primary visual or ophthalmologic causes, prompting repeat visual field testing, OCT, or neuro-ophthalmology referral instead of dementia evaluation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The face-recognition failure is associative agnosia from right anterior temporal degeneration, not a primary visual deficit. Visual acuity, fields, and extraocular movements are normal on neurological exam; object recognition and visuospatial function are intact. The ophthalmology evaluation is appropriately unremarkable.

red_herrings.data_point: Prior psychiatric diagnosis of major depressive disorder and ongoing sertraline 50 mg initiated 3 months ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could mislead the clinician into attributing all behavioral changes (apathy, social withdrawal, loss of interest) to undertreated or treatment-resistant depression, leading to antidepressant escalation rather than dementia evaluation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Apathy in FTD is not depression: the patient lacks subjective dysphoria, hopelessness, and neurovegetative features; behavioral symptoms including stereotypy, empathy loss, and prosopagnosia are not features of depression and do not respond to antidepressants. Progressive neuroimaging findings are incompatible with primary mood disorder.

metadata.notes: First right-temporal-predominant bvFTD in the NeuroBench v5 dataset. Cardinal feature is prosopagnosia (associative face agnosia from right anterior temporal degeneration). Teaching points: laterality discipline (right imaging = right-temporal cognitive signs), apathy-vs-depression trap, prosopagnosia localization. Two red herrings: ophthalmology-anchor and depression-attribution. Negative amyloid PET differentiates from atypical AD.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required tools (MRI, labs, neuropsych_battery, literature) plus recommended FDG-PET and optional amyloid PET; 2 embedded red herrings (ophthalmology-anchor and depression-attribution); requires multi-modal synthesis to distinguish right temporal FTD from atypical AD and primary visual disorder; face-localization knowledge tested.
